comparator.name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official study guide establishes a 180-EC bachelor with a common 60-EC first year and two equally weighted specialisations. The generic normalized target does not prefer one route. People, Planet, Power is selected through the neutral official-order tie-break. Its fixed 60-EC second year and 30-EC third-year core are reconstructed, Anthropology of Religion is the first-listed 10-EC exploration choice, and the genuine 30-EC free-elective space is preserved without invented content.

comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic bachelor and the official guide presents People, Planet, Power and Media Making Movements as equally weighted routes with a common first year. No route is shown as more representative of the whole degree, so the first-listed route is selected independently of UCR fit; its first-listed third-year exploration option, Anthropology of Religion, is used by the same neutral rule.

candidateAssessments.organisingLogic: The explicitly supplied candidate direction is “Ecology, Communities & Global Change”; its interest-row basis and disposition remain explicit in interestSelection.
candidateAssessments.assessment: The academic decision includes this candidate as ucr-2.

candidateAssessments.organisingLogic: The explicitly supplied candidate direction is “Media, Visual Culture & Digital Anthropology”; its interest-row basis and disposition remain explicit in interestSelection.
candidateAssessments.assessment: The academic decision includes this candidate as ucr-3.

People, Planet, Power and Media, Making, Movements are the two formal, evidence-backed specialisation directions and yield feasible, substantively distinct programmes. All generator-eligible interests are owned by the closest match or one of those two candidates, and the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both introduce systematic theoretical study of society and social organisation, although Leiden provides a dedicated anthropology-and-sociology sequence.
Both situate cultural and social change historically and transnationally.
Both develop qualitative research design, interviewing, observation, analysis and interpretation; Leiden adds dedicated anthropological field practice.
Both examine modern social theory, diversity, inequality and changing social relations.
Both engage advanced social theory about power, inequality and contemporary societies.
Both require sustained independent research and academic argument, though in different disciplinary settings.
Both use comparison to examine human communities and cultural difference, while archaeology and anthropology retain distinct methods.
UCR qualitative-methods study does not reproduce Leiden's separately credited ethnographic fieldwork component.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Leiden's multivariate-analysis component.
Both analyse states, citizenship, political institutions and power.
Both connect ecological challenges with social and economic systems; Leiden frames this anthropologically.
Both develop clear written argument and communication about cultural and social questions.
Both examine ethical foundations and responsibilities relevant to research on people and societies.
Both develop regionally grounded cultural analysis, though with distinct disciplinary objects and methods.
Both cultivate critical reading and interpretation of academic discourse and meaning.
Both use mediated and visual forms to analyse and communicate social life.
Both introduce quantitative analysis of data, while Leiden's component is oriented to anthropological and sociological research.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Anthropology of Religion.
Both support reflection on academic development, professional identity and future pathways.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Leiden's specialisation-specific research preparation.
Leiden's genuine 30-EC elective space remains open and is not replaced by invented content.

notes.text: Leiden provides a dedicated anthropology-and-development-sociology curriculum with sequenced anthropological theory, ethnographic methods and fieldwork. UCR can assemble strong cultural and qualitative social-science pathways, but does not reproduce that disciplinary sequence.
Leiden's 30-EC third-year free-elective space is retained without inventing a minor, exchange, internship or individual elective package.
